title: Where Does a Plant Add New Body?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Where Does a Plant Add New Body?' over a slowly turning silhouette of a large oak. COLOUR MAP used in both films, the take-homes and the text: dividing cells TEAL, elongating cells AMBER, mature cells GREEN; xylem and wood BROWN-GOLD, phloem VIOLET, cork DARK GREY. Cells are rounded rectangles, never molecular structures. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Where on a three-hundred-year-old oak were this spring's new leaves made? The tree is ancient, but this spring's leaves are only months old.
scenes.caption: Where on a 300-year-old oak were this spring's new leaves made? The tree is ancient, but this spring's leaves are only months old.
scenes.visual: The oak silhouette, labelled 'about 300 years old'. Fresh light-green leaves pop out along the twigs, each with a small tag 'this spring: months old'. A large question mark hovers over the crown.
scenes.narration: Where on a 300-year-old oak were this spring's new leaves made? The tree is ancient, but this spring's leaves are only months old.

scenes.tts: The answer is meristems. A meristem is a group of cells that keeps dividing. No adult mammal grows a new limb, but many plants keep their meristems for years. So they keep adding new organs.
scenes.visual: Camera pulls back to a young seedling silhouette. Small TEAL glowing points light up at the shoot tips and root tips, labelled 'meristem: cells that keep dividing'. A calendar strip flips through several years: new leaves appear beside the TEAL shoot tips; new side roots emerge a little behind the root tips, and each new side root gets its own TEAL tip once it is out.
scenes.narration: The answer is meristems. A meristem is a group of cells that keeps dividing. No adult mammal grows a new limb, but many plants keep their meristems for years. So they keep adding new organs.

scenes.tts: Apical meristems sit at the tips of growing roots and shoots. Growth from them is called primary growth. It is mainly growth in length.
scenes.visual: The TEAL tip points pulse. Arrows from the shoot tip point up and from the root tips point down, labelled 'apical meristems: primary growth, mainly length'. The rest of the seedling body stays still and grey-green.
scenes.narration: Apical meristems sit at the tips of growing roots and shoots. Growth from them is called primary growth. It is mainly growth in length.

scenes.tts: Zoom in on a root tip. A root cap shields the front as it pushes through soil. Just behind the cap, small cells divide. This is the zone of division.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a root tip shown as a column of rounded-rectangle cells. A pale cap at the very front, labelled 'root cap'. Behind it a short band of small TEAL cells splitting in two, labelled 'zone of division'. Soil grains slide past the tip.
scenes.narration: Zoom in on a root tip. A root cap shields the front as it pushes through soil. Just behind the cap, small cells divide. This is the zone of division.

scenes.tts: A little further back, division tapers off. Cells lengthen many times over as water fills their vacuoles, the big water sacs inside them. This is the zone of elongation.
scenes.visual: Behind the TEAL band, cells turn AMBER and stretch lengthwise as a pale blue water-filled vacuole inside each one swells, labelled 'vacuole'. Label 'zone of elongation'. A small on-screen tag: 'about 20 times longer (illustrative)'.
scenes.narration: A little further back, division tapers off. Cells lengthen many times over as water fills their vacuoles, the big water sacs inside them. This is the zone of elongation.

scenes.tts: Further back still, cells stop lengthening. They take on their final types, and root hairs grow out from the surface. This is the zone of maturation.
scenes.visual: Further back, AMBER cells turn GREEN and stop changing size. Fine root hairs sprout from the outer GREEN cells. Label 'zone of maturation'. All three zone labels now sit side by side along the root.
scenes.narration: Further back still, cells stop lengthening. They take on their final types, and root hairs grow out from the surface. This is the zone of maturation.

scenes.tts: Now follow one lengthwise row of cells, a cell file. New cells leave the meristem at a steady rhythm. Each one stretches, then stops. Meanwhile the tip keeps moving forward through the soil.
scenes.visual: One cell file highlighted as a conveyor. TEAL cells pop off the meristem with a ticking metronome, turn AMBER and stretch, then turn GREEN and freeze. The cap and TEAL zone slide steadily forward through the soil while the GREEN region stays fixed relative to the soil.
scenes.narration: Now follow one lengthwise row of cells, a cell file. New cells leave the meristem at a steady rhythm. Each one stretches, then stops. Meanwhile the tip keeps moving forward through the soil.

scenes.tts: Paint ink marks at even spacing along a growing root tip. A day later, which gaps between the marks have widened?
scenes.visual: Evenly spaced black ink marks painted across the root, from the cap back into the GREEN region. A clock icon reads '1 day later?'. The marks hold still.
scenes.narration: Paint ink marks at even spacing along a growing root tip. A day later, which gaps between the marks have widened?

scenes.visual: The marked root holds still with a large question mark beside it. Small on-screen text: 'Which gaps widen?'.

scenes.tts: Mostly the gaps in the zone of elongation, where cells stretch. In the mature region, where cells have stopped lengthening, the marks stay put.
scenes.visual: The day plays out (schematic): gaps over the AMBER zone stretch wide; gaps over the GREEN zone do not change at all. Labels: 'widened' over AMBER, 'no change' over GREEN.
scenes.narration: Mostly the gaps in the zone of elongation, where cells stretch. In the mature region, where cells have stopped lengthening, the marks stay put.

scenes.tts: So how fast does the root grow? Count the new cells each file makes per hour. Multiply by the final length each cell reaches.
scenes.visual: The rule writes itself on screen: 'growth per hour = new cells per file per hour x final cell length'. The first term is underlined in TEAL, the second in AMBER. The conveyor keeps ticking behind it.
scenes.narration: So how fast does the root grow? Count the new cells each file makes per hour. Multiply by the final length each cell reaches.

scenes.tts: That product is the growth rate. It holds at steady state, when the zones keep their size and every file behaves alike.
scenes.visual: Under the rule, a small grey scope tag: 'steady state: zones keep their size; every cell file alike'. Several parallel cell files run in step, identical.
scenes.narration: That product is the growth rate. It holds at steady state, when the zones keep their size and every file behaves alike.

scenes.tts: Now block stretching but leave division alone. Cells keep coming, yet the tip barely creeps forward. Most of a root's new length comes from stretching, not from dividing.
scenes.visual: The AMBER stretch freezes: cells leave the meristem and stay short. The TEAL conveyor keeps ticking, but the tip's forward motion slows to a crawl. On-screen tag: 'growth falls to 1/20 of normal (illustrative numbers)'.
scenes.narration: Now block stretching but leave division alone. Cells keep coming, yet the tip barely creeps forward. Most of a root's new length comes from stretching, not from dividing.

scenes.tts: A shoot tip grows the same way, though it has no cap. At each node it adds one or more leaves, with a bud in the angle of each leaf.
scenes.visual: Cut to a shoot tip in silhouette, TEAL at the apex, no cap. As it rises, leaves unfold at each node (one here; a small inset shows a species with two leaves per node), each with a small TEAL bud in the angle between leaf and stem; labels 'node', 'internode', 'bud'.
scenes.narration: A shoot tip grows the same way, though it has no cap. At each node it adds one or more leaves, with a bud in the angle of each leaf.

scenes.tts: So a plant's new cells come from its meristems. For a root at steady state, growth equals new cells per file per hour, times their final length.
scenes.visual: Back to the whole oak: TEAL points glow at the shoot and root tips while the rule from s11 fades in beneath it, with its grey tag 'root, steady state, per cell file'. The trunk sits in the foreground, untouched by the TEAL points.
scenes.narration: So a plant's new cells come from its meristems. For a root at steady state, growth equals new cells per file per hour, times their final length.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'At steady state, root growth = cells per file per hour × final length.'
